# Diffusion and Flow Matching {#sec-diffusion}

Everything in this book so far generates by predicting the next token. The
image, audio, and video models that @sec-beyond-text gestures at mostly do not:
they start from pure noise and remove it. This chapter teaches that family,
diffusion and its flow-matching generalization, because it is the generative
principle behind almost all non-text media and is now reaching back into text. By
the end a reader can explain why generation-by-denoising sidesteps the
left-to-right constraint of autoregression, how a fixed noising process defines a
learned reverse one, why training reduces to predicting noise, what made latent
diffusion affordable, how flow matching reframed the whole thing as learning a
velocity field, and why the frontier is collapsing a thousand sampling steps
toward one.

## Why not autoregression

Autoregressive generation is sequential by construction: one token after another,
left to right, a serial chain whose length is the output. For text that ordering
is natural. For an image it is not: pixels have no canonical order, and forcing
one wastes the structure. Diffusion takes a different route. Corrupt data into
noise by a fixed, known process, then learn to reverse it, denoising the whole
signal in parallel at each step. There is no left-to-right, the output size is
fixed up front, and the model can attend to the entire partially-denoised signal
at once.

## The forward and reverse processes

The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to a datum over $T$ steps until
little but noise remains, a fixed Markov chain with no parameters. Generation
runs it backwards, learning to undo one noising step at a time. The surprise of
Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models is that this reverse process has a
simple trainable form: the network is trained to predict the noise
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ that was added to a sample at a randomly chosen step
[@ho2020ddpm], an ordinary regression,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{\,t,\,\mathbf{x}_0,\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
\left\lVert \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\!\left(
\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\; t
\right) \right\rVert^2,
$$

where $\bar{\alpha}_t$ is the surviving signal fraction at step $t$. Sampling
starts from pure noise and applies the learned denoiser step by step. The toy
below makes the loop concrete: for one-dimensional Gaussian data the optimal
noise-predictor is analytic, so we can sample from noise and watch the
distribution come back.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

mu, v0 = 3.0, 1.0                          # data ~ N(mu, v0)
T = 1000
beta = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)         # noise schedule
alpha = 1 - beta
abar = np.cumprod(alpha)                   # surviving signal fraction

def eps_star(x, t):                        # optimal epsilon-prediction (analytic)
    var = abar[t] * v0 + (1 - abar[t])
    return np.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * (x - np.sqrt(abar[t]) * mu) / var

x = rng.normal(size=5000)                  # start from pure noise
for t in range(T - 1, -1, -1):
    mean = (x - beta[t] / np.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * eps_star(x, t)) / np.sqrt(alpha[t])
    x = mean + (np.sqrt(beta[t]) * rng.normal(size=x.shape) if t > 0 else 0.0)

print(f"data N(mu={mu}, var={v0});  samples: mean={x.mean():.2f}, var={x.var():.2f}")
```
::::

## One framework: scores and SDEs

A second lineage arrived at the same place from a different direction. Score-based
models learn the score, the gradient of the log-density, at many noise levels and
sample by Langevin dynamics [@song2019ncsn]. Song et al. then showed the two are
one thing: the forward process is a stochastic differential equation that carries
data to noise, generation is the reverse-time SDE, and both DDPM and
score-matching are discretizations of it [@song2020sde]. The same work derives an
equivalent deterministic probability-flow ODE with the same marginals, and that
ODE is the bridge to fast samplers and to flow matching below.

## Making it cheap and steerable

Three moves turned a slow research method into a deployed one. Fewer steps came
first: DDIM is a non-Markovian sampler that reaches comparable quality 10 to 50
times faster, and is deterministic when its noise term is set to zero
[@song2020ddim]. Affordability came from latent diffusion, which runs the whole
process in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder rather than on pixels,
cutting compute by a large factor, and injects text or layout through
cross-attention, the recipe behind Stable Diffusion [@rombach2022ldm]. Control
came from classifier-free guidance: train one model jointly with and without the
conditioning signal by dropping it part of the time, then at sampling extrapolate
between the conditional and unconditional predictions by a guidance weight,
trading diversity for fidelity with no separate classifier [@ho2022cfg]. The
backbone then caught up with the rest of the book: DiT replaces the U-Net with a
transformer over latent patches and finds that sample quality falls as compute
rises, putting diffusion on the same scaling curve as everything else
[@peebles2022dit].

## Flow matching: learn a velocity, not a denoiser

Flow matching reframes the problem. Instead of a denoiser, learn a vector field
that transports noise to data along a fixed conditional probability path, trained
simulation-free by regressing onto that field, with the diffusion paths falling
out as one special case and straight optimal-transport paths as a more efficient
other [@lipman2022fm]. Rectified flow pushes the idea to its useful extreme:
learn straight-line transport between noise and data, which lets an Euler sampler
take very few steps, even one, and a recursive "rectification" keeps straightening
the trajectories [@liu2022rectified]. Consistency models collapse the path
entirely, training a network that maps any point on the probability-flow ODE
trajectory directly to its origin, so one forward pass generates a sample, either
distilled from a diffusion teacher or trained standalone [@song2023consistency].
The arc across this section is a single quantity coming down: the number of
sequential network evaluations a sample costs.

## The loop back to language

Diffusion is now returning to text. LLaDA trains a language model from scratch
with a masked-denoising diffusion objective, predicting masked tokens by a
reverse process rather than left to right, and reports it competitive with an
autoregressive LLaMA3-8B at in-context learning [@nie2025llada]. The appeal is
parallel, bidirectional decoding and an escape from strict left-to-right order;
the open question is whether the approach scales to the frontier.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether non-autoregressive diffusion language models can match autoregressive
LLMs at scale is unsettled. LLaDA shows competitiveness at 8B, but against the
authors' own controlled baselines rather than external frontier models, and the
strongest "surpasses" result is narrow, a reversal task GPT-4o handles poorly
[@nie2025llada]. The case for diffusion text rests on parallel decoding and
bidirectional context; the case against is that autoregression still owns every
frontier model and has the more mature scaling and serving story. Treat
diffusion for language as promising and unproven above small scale.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The sampler's step count is a serving-cost lever that reaches back into the
training objective. A thousand-step DDPM is too slow to serve at scale, so the
field trains specifically for few-step sampling, rectified flow's straight paths
and consistency distillation, rather than treating sampling as an afterthought.
The inference budget per image, paid on every generation, dictates which
generative objective is worth training, the same constraint @sec-scaling-laws
draws for tokens, here drawn for denoising steps.
:::
